KM_T_01.name: Immediately effective kamma
KM_T_01.description: Kamma that produces its result in the same life; if it cannot mature, it becomes defunct.
KM_T_01.doctrinalNote: Kamma that produces its result in the same life; if it cannot mature, it becomes defunct.

KM_T_02.name: Subsequently effective kamma
KM_T_02.description: Kamma that produces its result in the immediately following life.
KM_T_02.doctrinalNote: Kamma that produces its result in the immediately following life.

KM_T_03.name: Indefinitely effective kamma
KM_T_03.description: Kamma capable of producing results from the third life onward until final liberation.
KM_T_03.doctrinalNote: Kamma capable of producing results from the third life onward until final liberation.

KM_T_04.name: Defunct kamma
KM_T_04.description: Kamma whose opportunity to produce a result has passed.
KM_T_04.doctrinalNote: Kamma whose opportunity to produce a result has passed.

KM_P_01.name: Reproductive kamma
KM_P_01.description: Kamma that generates rebirth and the resultant aggregates of a new life.
KM_P_01.doctrinalNote: Kamma that generates rebirth and the resultant aggregates of a new life.

KM_P_02.name: Supportive kamma
KM_P_02.description: Kamma that supports and sustains the result of another kamma.
KM_P_02.doctrinalNote: Kamma that supports and sustains the result of another kamma.

KM_P_03.name: Obstructive kamma
KM_P_03.description: Kamma that obstructs or weakens the result of another kamma.
KM_P_03.doctrinalNote: Kamma that obstructs or weakens the result of another kamma.

KM_P_04.name: Destructive kamma
KM_P_04.description: Kamma that cuts off the result of another kamma and replaces it with its own result.
KM_P_04.doctrinalNote: Kamma that cuts off the result of another kamma and replaces it with its own result.

KM_U_01.name: Weighty kamma
KM_U_01.description: A very powerful wholesome or unwholesome kamma that takes priority in producing rebirth.
KM_U_01.doctrinalNote: A very powerful wholesome or unwholesome kamma that takes priority in producing rebirth.

KM_U_02.name: Death-proximate kamma
KM_U_02.description: Kamma remembered or performed close to death, influencing the next rebirth.
KM_U_02.doctrinalNote: Kamma remembered or performed close to death, influencing the next rebirth.

KM_U_03.name: Habitual kamma
KM_U_03.description: Kamma repeatedly performed until it becomes a strong habit.
KM_U_03.doctrinalNote: Kamma repeatedly performed until it becomes a strong habit.

KM_U_04.name: Cumulative kamma
KM_U_04.description: Accumulated kamma that produces a result when no stronger kamma takes priority.
KM_U_04.doctrinalNote: Accumulated kamma that produces a result when no stronger kamma takes priority.

KM_R_01.name: Unwholesome kamma
KM_R_01.description: Unwholesome kamma producing suffering - 12 unwholesome cittas produce 7 unwholesome rootless resultants and rebirth in 4 woeful planes.
KM_R_01.doctrinalNote: Akusala-kamma is the cause of dukkha, belonging to sense-sphere, resulting in woeful planes.

KM_R_02.name: Sense-sphere wholesome kamma
KM_R_02.description: Wholesome sense-sphere kamma producing happy sense-sphere results - 8 great wholesome cittas produce 8 great resultants and 7 wholesome rootless, rebirth as human or 6 deva planes.
KM_R_02.doctrinalNote: Kusala Duggati: wholesome resulting in happy sense-sphere, foundation for all merit.

KM_R_03.name: Form-sphere wholesome kamma
KM_R_03.description: Wholesome form-sphere kamma (5 form jhanas) producing form-sphere results - rebirth in 16 Brahma form planes, result is 5 form-sphere resultant cittas.
KM_R_03.doctrinalNote: Rupavacara-kamma belongs to exalted, beyond sense-sphere, giving result corresponding to jhana attained.

KM_R_04.name: Supramundane kamma (Path kamma)
KM_R_04.description: Supramundane kamma is the 4 Path cittas (Magga) - eradicating defilements and giving supramundane results as 4 Fruition cittas (Phala) and Nibbana, ending samsara.
KM_R_04.doctrinalNote: Lokuttara-kamma does not give rebirth in three planes but gives Nibbana - ultimate goal of VDP.

PD_01.name: Ignorance
PD_01.description: Ignorance is not knowing the Four Noble Truths, the three characteristics, kamma and its results, and dependent origination. It is the first root of the round of rebirth: without ignorance formations do not arise and the chain of dependent arising cannot form.
PD_01.characteristic: Not understanding — blindness to the true nature of things (the Four Truths, the three characteristics).
PD_01.function: To obscure clear seeing, and to serve as condition for the arising of formations.
PD_01.manifestation: As bewilderment and darkness — it keeps generating kamma (formations) without one realising it.
PD_01.proximateCause: Unwise attention (ayoniso-manasikāra); not meeting the wise and not hearing the True Dhamma.
PD_01.doctrinalNote: Avijjā has no discernible beginning (anamatagga). The ending of ignorance is the attainment of the four path consciousnesses.
examples: Not knowing this body is impermanent, one clings to it as a self and creates kamma to protect that self.

PD_02.name: Volitional formations
PD_02.description: Formations are kamma-forming activities — volition (cetanā) through the three doors of body, speech, and mind. They are of three kinds: meritorious formations (wholesome), demeritorious formations (unwholesome), and imperturbable formations (meditative attainments).
PD_02.characteristic: Acting and arranging — deliberate formation through body, speech, and mind.
PD_02.function: To generate kamma — accumulating kammic force that will yield rebirth in a future life.
PD_02.manifestation: As accumulated kamma that will draw consciousness into rebirth.
PD_02.proximateCause: Ignorance as condition (without ignorance, formations become supramundane and create no new kamma).
PD_02.doctrinalNote: Saṅkhārā in dependent origination means the volition (cetanā) mental factor that forms kamma.
examples: Giving with a wholesome mind is a meritorious formation; its consciousness rebirth-links into a good destination.
Attaining jhāna is an imperturbable formation; its consciousness rebirth-links as a Brahmā.

PD_03.name: Consciousness
PD_03.description: Consciousness here means chiefly the rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhi-citta) — the first mind of this life, continuing from the previous life and carrying kamma's seed.
PD_03.characteristic: Knowing an object — the rebirth consciousness resting on the new mind-and-matter.
PD_03.function: To rebirth — to open a new life.
PD_03.manifestation: A new existence takes shape — mind-and-matter appear.
PD_03.proximateCause: Kamma (formations) as condition; mind-and-matter must be there to rest on.
PD_03.doctrinalNote: Consciousness and mind-and-matter lean on each other — like two sheaves of reeds propping one another up.
examples: At the moment of conception the rebirth-linking consciousness appears, mind-and-matter develop, and a new life begins.

PD_04.name: Mind and matter
PD_04.description: Mind-and-matter is the whole psycho-physical person: materiality (the body — the four great essentials and derived materiality) and mentality (consciousness together with its mental factors).
PD_04.characteristic: Existing — mind and body present and developing.
PD_04.function: To serve as the ground on which consciousness operates, and the condition for the six sense bases to develop.
PD_04.manifestation: The six sense bases become fully formed.
PD_04.proximateCause: Consciousness as condition; the four sources producing materiality.
examples: In the womb: rebirth consciousness appears and mind-and-matter gradually develop from embryo to full term.

PD_05.name: Six sense bases
PD_05.description: The six sense bases are the six places where objects are received: the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind bases — six doors through which the mind receives the six objects.
PD_05.characteristic: Readiness to receive — six doors through which objects enter.
PD_05.function: To serve as doors (dvāra) through which the mind meets outer objects.
PD_05.manifestation: Contact (phassa) is established — the mind can touch its object.
examples: A newborn child: with the six bases complete, contact with the outside world begins.

PD_06.name: Contact
PD_06.description: Contact is the meeting of three factors: sense base + object + consciousness. It is the condition for feeling to arise.
PD_06.characteristic: Touching — the encounter of base, object, and consciousness.
PD_06.function: To gather base, object, and consciousness together — conditioning the arising of feeling.
PD_06.manifestation: Mind, mental factors, base, and object come together.
PD_06.proximateCause: All three must be present: base + object + consciousness.
PD_06.doctrinalNote: Phassa in dependent origination is the contact mental factor (CS_PHASSA).
examples: The eye sees a lovely object: eye-base + visible object + eye-consciousness give eye-contact, and glad feeling follows.

PD_07.name: Feeling
PD_07.description: Feeling is the experience that follows contact — glad, sad, pleasant, painful, or neutral. This is the most important point of meditation practice: stop at feeling, and do not let feeling lead on to craving.
PD_07.characteristic: Experiencing — tasting the object as pleasant, painful, or neutral after contact.
PD_07.function: To enjoy the object — conditioning craving to arise when unwise attention prevails.
PD_07.manifestation: As pleasant, painful, or neutral experience forming in the mind.
PD_07.doctrinalNote: This is the crux of the four foundations of mindfulness: halt at feeling, and do not let it ripen into craving.
examples: Hearing praise (contact) brings glad feeling; without mindfulness, craving for more follows.

PD_08.name: Craving
PD_08.description: Craving is thirst, the intense wanting. It is of three kinds: craving for sense pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence. Craving is the Truth of the Origin — the root of suffering.
PD_08.characteristic: Thirsting — the clinging wanting produced by feeling.
PD_08.function: To grasp at its object — conditioning the arising of clinging.
PD_08.manifestation: As clinging taking hold; the round of rebirth continues.
PD_08.proximateCause: Feeling (especially glad and pleasant feeling) as condition.
PD_08.doctrinalNote: Craving is the Origin of suffering among the Four Noble Truths. The ending of craving is the ending of suffering — Nibbāna.
examples: Seeing delicious food, craving arises: wanting to eat more.
Meeting pain, craving for non-existence arises: wanting not to be.

PD_09.name: Clinging
PD_09.description: Clinging is grasping tighter than craving. It is of four kinds: clinging to sense pleasures, to views, to rules and observances, and to a doctrine of self.
PD_09.characteristic: Holding tight — a grip that does not let go.
PD_09.function: To grasp the object firmly — conditioning the arising of becoming.
PD_09.manifestation: As becoming taking shape — rebirth-producing kamma accumulates.
PD_09.proximateCause: Craving as condition — clinging is craving intensified and consolidated.
examples: Not only wanting money (craving) but being unable to let money go (clinging).

PD_10.name: Becoming
PD_10.description: Becoming has two parts: kamma-becoming (kamma accumulated that will produce rebirth) and rebirth-becoming (the plane of existence into which rebirth will occur). There are three realms of becoming: sense-sphere, form-sphere, and formless-sphere becoming.
PD_10.characteristic: Existing — accumulated kammic force ready to produce rebirth.
PD_10.function: To condition birth taking place in a future life.
PD_10.manifestation: As rebirth occurring in a plane that matches the kamma.
PD_10.proximateCause: Clinging as condition — clinging is the fuel for becoming.
examples: One who gives generously all their life builds wholesome sense-sphere becoming and is reborn wealthy in the next life.

PD_11.name: Birth
PD_11.description: Birth is rebirth — the rebirth-linking consciousness appearing in a new life, mind-and-matter forming, the aggregates arising. All suffering begins here.
PD_11.characteristic: Rebirth-linking — consciousness reborn into a new plane.
PD_11.function: To open a new life — dragging the whole mass of suffering along.
PD_11.doctrinalNote: The three-life circle joins here: birth (PD_11) corresponds to consciousness (PD_03) on the result side of the future life.
examples: The moment of conception is birth — all suffering follows from it.

PD_12.name: Ageing and death
PD_12.description: Ageing-and-death: ageing is growing old and decaying; death is falling. Together with them come sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair — all the suffering of a life. It is the final result that closes one life and, if there is no liberation, opens a new round.
PD_12.characteristic: Ageing and dying — the inevitable decay and perishing of all conditioned mind and body.
PD_12.function: To end a life — and to continue a new round of becoming if liberation has not been won.
PD_12.manifestation: A life closed; without liberation the round continues.
PD_12.proximateCause: Birth as condition — where there is birth, ageing-and-death necessarily follow.
PD_12.doctrinalNote: Liberation means ending ignorance (PD_01) and craving (PD_08) — the realisation of Nibbāna.
examples: Every being that has been born must age and die.
When ignorance and craving are destroyed, ageing-and-death no longer follow.

VT_NGU_MON_RATLON.name: Atimahanta-ārammaṇa Pañcadvāra-vīthi
VT_NGU_MON_RATLON.description: The most complete process — it arises when a five-sense object strikes very strongly. All 17 mind-moments occur: 2 vibrating and 1 arresting bhavaṅga, 5 rootless cittas, 7 impulsions, and 2 registrations.
VT_NGU_MON_RATLON.arisingCondition: A five-sense object (visible form, sound, odour, taste, tangibility) strikes its corresponding sense base very strongly.
VT_NGU_MON_RATLON.significance: The most complete process — the 7 impulsions create kamma in full, and registration enjoys the residual object.
VT_NGU_MON_RATLON.doctrinalNote: Atimahanta = an object great enough to allow Javana × 7 plus Tadārammaṇa × 2.

1.name: Past bhavaṅga
1.description: The life-continuum flowing along normally before the object strikes.
1.doctrinalNote: The same class of citta as this person's rebirth-linking and dying consciousness.

2.name: Vibrating bhavaṅga
2.description: The object strikes the sense base and the life-continuum vibrates for the first time.

3.name: Arrest bhavaṅga
3.description: The bhavaṅga stream is fully cut off — the cognitive process begins.
3.doctrinalNote: After this moment the five-door adverting consciousness arises.

4.name: Five-door adverting
4.description: Opens the five-sense door and turns toward the object, determining which door the object has struck.
4.doctrinalNote: CI_028 — equanimity feeling, 11 mental factors. Creates no kamma.

5.name: Five-fold sense consciousness
5.description: Knows the object through the corresponding sense door. Only the seven universal mental factors accompany it.
5.doctrinalNote: Unwholesome-resultant (CI_013–017) or wholesome-resultant (CI_020–024), according to rebirth kamma.

6.name: Receiving
6.description: Receives the object from the sense consciousness and passes it into the inner stream of consciousness.
6.doctrinalNote: CI_018 = unwholesome-resultant with equanimity; CI_025 = wholesome-resultant with equanimity. 10 mental factors.

7.name: Investigating
7.description: Examines the object — determining whether it is good or bad, pleasing or not.
7.doctrinalNote: CI_027 (with joy) appears only when the object is very beautiful.

8.name: Determining
8.description: Makes the final determination of the object as good or bad — opening the way for the 7 impulsions.
8.doctrinalNote: CI_029 (mind-door adverting) plays the role of determining. 11 mental factors. It decides the kind of javana that follows.

9.name: Impulsion (Javana)
9.description: Seven consecutive impulsion moments — creating wholesome or unwholesome kamma. Moment 1 bears fruit in this very life; moment 7 in the next life; moments 2–6 in later lives.
9.doctrinalNote: 7 moments of one and the same class of citta. The only part of the process that creates kamma.

10.name: Registration (Tadārammaṇa)
10.description: Two registration moments enjoying the residual object after the impulsions. They occur only in a very-great-object process and create no new kamma.
10.doctrinalNote: Tadā = 'then'; ārammaṇa = object. They arise only when the object is great enough.

11.name: Post-process bhavaṅga
11.description: After the process ends, the life-continuum resumes its normal flow.

VT_NGU_MON_LON.name: Mahanta-ārammaṇa Pañcadvāra-vīthi
VT_NGU_MON_LON.description: A five-door process with the full 7 impulsions but NO registration — the object is not strong enough for tadārammaṇa to arise.
VT_NGU_MON_LON.arisingCondition: A five-sense object strong enough for 7 impulsions, but not strong enough to produce registration.
VT_NGU_MON_LON.significance: The most ordinary process — kamma is created in full through the 7 impulsions.
VT_NGU_MON_LON.doctrinalNote: It differs from the very-great-object process only in lacking the 2 registration moments.

1.name: Vibrating bhavaṅga
1.description: The life-continuum vibrates as the object strikes the sense base.

2.name: Arrest bhavaṅga
2.description: The bhavaṅga stream is cut off — the process begins.

3.name: Five-door adverting
3.description: Turns the mind toward the object through the five-sense door.

4.name: Five-fold sense consciousness
4.description: Knows the object through the corresponding sense.

7.name: Determining
7.description: Determines the object, opening the way for the impulsions.

8.name: Impulsion (Javana)
8.description: Seven impulsion moments create kamma. Afterwards there is NO registration.
8.doctrinalNote: After the 7 impulsions the mind drops straight back into the life-continuum.

9.name: Post-process bhavaṅga
9.description: The life-continuum resumes after the process.

VT_Y_MON.name: Manodvāra-vīthi
VT_Y_MON.description: The mind-door process arises when the mind contacts a mind object through the mind door — thinking, remembering, imagining. Immediately after the mind-door adverting consciousness come the 7 impulsions.
VT_Y_MON.arisingCondition: A mind object (dhammārammaṇa) appears at the mind door — a thought, a memory, an imagination.
VT_Y_MON.significance: It explains all inner mental activity. It creates mind-kamma, and is the wellspring of verbal and bodily kamma.
VT_Y_MON.doctrinalNote: The mind-door process begins with the mind-door adverting consciousness (CI_029), without passing through five-door adverting.

1.name: Vibrating bhavaṅga
1.description: The life-continuum vibrates as the mind object strikes.

2.name: Arrest bhavaṅga
2.description: The life-continuum is arrested — the mind-door process begins.

3.name: Mind-door adverting
3.description: Opens the mind door and directs the mind to the mind object, at the same time determining it (serving as determining within this process).
3.doctrinalNote: CI_029 serves both as mind-door adverting and as determining. 11 mental factors.

4.name: Impulsion (Javana)
4.description: Seven impulsion moments — creating mind-kamma. All deliberate thought, speech, and action arise here.
4.doctrinalNote: Creates mind-kamma directly. Verbal and bodily kamma also begin at the mind door.

5.name: Registration (optional)
5.description: Registration in the mind-door process — depending on the strength of the mind object.

VT_VITHIMUTTA.name: Vīthimutta-citta
VT_VITHIMUTTA.description: Vīthimutta are consciousnesses operating outside the cognitive process — through no door at all. They have three functions: rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi), life-continuum (bhavaṅga), and death (cuti). All three use the same type of consciousness.
VT_VITHIMUTTA.arisingCondition: Rebirth-linking: when the previous life ends. Life-continuum: between processes. Death: when the material life faculty perishes.
VT_VITHIMUTTA.significance: It explains the mechanism of rebirth and the linkage between lives.
VT_VITHIMUTTA.doctrinalNote: Process-free consciousness creates no new kamma — it is kammically indeterminate resultant mind.

1.name: Rebirth-linking consciousness
1.description: The first consciousness of the new life — continuing directly from the previous life's dying consciousness, carrying kamma's seed.
1.doctrinalNote: CI_019/CI_026 = a two-rooted person; CI_027 = a specially favoured person; CI_063–CI_070 = a three-rooted person or a deva.

2.name: Life-continuum consciousness
2.description: The stream of consciousness that sustains the life between processes. It arises and passes innumerable times, and is the foundation of all mental activity.
2.doctrinalNote: Bhavaṅga = the life-maintaining part of the stream. It runs in deep sleep and between processes.

3.name: Death consciousness
3.description: The final mind-moment — the material life faculty perishes, the death consciousness falls, and the life ends. Immediately afterwards the next life's rebirth-linking consciousness arises.
3.doctrinalNote: Cuti = to move on, to depart. The object of the death consciousness is the death-proximate (āsanna) object.

M1_BASICS.title: Seven universal cetasikas
M1_BASICS.description: The seven mental factors present in every citta; the foundation for all later modules.

lessonSections.title: The Aññasamāna group and the universal factors
body: This paragraph explains the relevant Dhamma as taught in the source.
The Aññasamāna group is divided into two: the universal factors (Sabbacittasādhāraṇa), seven in number, and the occasional factors (Pakiṇṇaka), six in number.
The seven universal mental factors are: Contact (Phassa), Feeling (Vedanā), Perception (Saññā), Volition (Cetanā), One-pointedness (Ekaggatā), Life faculty (Jīvitindriya) and Attention (Manasikāra).
They are called 'universal' because all seven arise together with every citta without exception.

sourceRefs.note: TÂM SỞ TỢ THA – AÑÑASAMĀNA; liệt kê Biến hành 7 và Biệt cảnh 6

lessonSections.title: Contact (Phassa) and Feeling (Vedanā)
body: Phassa comes from the root 'phas' — to touch, to contact, to impinge. Whenever consciousness meets its object, the mental factor of contact is present.

In the five-aggregate existence, when a sense base (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body) meets its corresponding object (visible form, sound, odour, taste, tangible object) consciousness arises — at that moment contact is present. Each base contacts only its own object.
In the four-mental-aggregate existence (the immaterial sphere, where no materiality exists), contact requires only object and consciousness impinging on each other.
Vedanā comes from the root 'vid' — to feel, to experience. When an object impinges on the mental stream, feeling receives and experiences that object.
An important relationship: contact is nutriment for feeling — because of contact, feeling arises; hence it is called 'contact as nutriment' (phassa-āhāra).

sourceRefs.note: I.1/ TÂM SỞ XÚC – PHASSA
Xúc phân theo cõi và theo hướng
I.2/ TÂM SỞ THỌ – VEDANĀ; Xúc là vật thực cho Thọ

lessonSections.title: Perception (Saññā) and Volition (Cetanā)
body: Saññā = saṃ + ñā: to know what has been known before, to remember and recognise something through its mark.
Perception is classified by kind into three: unwholesome, wholesome and indeterminate; and by object into six (form-perception, sound-perception, etc.).
Cetanā, citta and cetasika all derive from the root 'cit' — to think, to consider. Volition is the most important mental factor.
The special task of volition is twofold: it performs its own function and it organises the activity of the other co-arisen mental factors — and it is volition that creates kamma.

sourceRefs.note: I.3/ TÂM SỞ TƯỞNG – SAÑÑĀ
I.4/ TÂM SỞ TƯ – CETANĀ, nhiệm vụ đặc biệt, tạo nghiệp

lessonSections.title: One-pointedness, Life faculty and Attention
body: Ekaggatā: eka (one) + agga (peak) — one-pointedness, concentration. It gathers citta and its co-arisen mental factors onto a single object, holding the mind steady without wavering.
Jīvitindriya: jīvita (life, maintaining) + indriya (faculty, controlling). The life faculty governs the existence of co-arisen phenomena.

There are two kinds: mental life faculty maintains mentality for three sub-moments (arising, presence, dissolution); material life faculty maintains materiality for 51 sub-moments (17 mind-moments × 3).
Manasikāra: manasī (mind) + kāra (making) — making in the mind, i.e., attention. It gathers the object to make it the citta's object.

The fourfold definition of attention: characteristic — directing associated phenomena to the object; function — yoking co-arisen mind and mental factors to the object; manifestation — facing the object; proximate cause — the object.

sourceRefs.note: I.5/ TÂM SỞ NHẤT HÀNH (ĐỊNH) – EKAGGATĀ
I.6/ TÂM SỞ MẠNG QUYỀN – JĪVITINDRIYA; 3 và 51 sát na tiểu
7/ TÂM SỞ TÁC Ý – MANASIKĀRA; tứ ý nghĩa

reviewCards.back: Root 'phas': to touch, to contact, to encounter the object.

reviewCards.front: How is Saññā etymologically derived?
reviewCards.back: saññā = saṃ + ñā: to know what has been known before, to remember through a mark.

reviewCards.front: From which common root do Cetanā, Citta and Cetasika derive?
reviewCards.back: Root 'cit': to think, to consider.

reviewCards.front: Why is Volition (Cetanā) the most important mental factor?
reviewCards.back: Because Volition organises the activity of co-arisen mental factors and it is volition that creates kamma.

reviewCards.front: How is Ekaggatā etymologically derived?
reviewCards.back: eka = one, agga = peak → one-pointedness, concentration.

reviewCards.front: How long does mental life faculty maintain mentality?
reviewCards.back: Three sub-moments: arising, presence, dissolution.

reviewCards.front: How long does material life faculty maintain materiality?
reviewCards.back: 51 sub-moments = 17 mind-moments × 3 sub-moments.

reviewCards.front: How is Manasikāra etymologically derived?
reviewCards.back: Manasī: mind + kāra: making → making in the mind, attention.

reviewCards.front: What is the function of Attention (Manasikāra)?
reviewCards.back: It yokes co-arisen mind and mental factors to grasp the object.

lessonSections.title: The occasional factors within Aññasamāna
body: This paragraph explains Aññasamāna: its characteristic, function, manifestation and proximate cause as taught in the Abhidhamma.

lessonSections.title: Initial application (Vitakka) and Sustained application (Vicāra)
body: Vitakka comes from 'vi' (special) + root 'takk' (to think) — initial application, special thinking. Its characteristic is lifting co-arisen mental factors onto the object.
This section presents the Abhidhamma teaching on the relevant mental factors: their definitions, classifications and relationships as preserved in the source material.
This section presents the Abhidhamma teaching on the relevant mental factors: their definitions, classifications and relationships as preserved in the source material.

Vicāra comes from 'vi' + 'car' (to wander) — sustained application that keeps the mind continuously on the object, examining it. Vitakka is like a bee flying to the lotus, vicāra like the bee circling it.
Traditional similes: vitakka is like a bee flying to a lotus, a bird taking off, striking a drum; vicāra is like the bee circling the lotus, the bird soaring, the drum's resonance.

Initial and sustained application are absent from the five pairs of sense consciousnesses (ten cittas), because those sense consciousnesses function automatically through impingement and need no thinking.

M2_SI_PHAN.title: The delusion group
M2_SI_PHAN.description: Delusion, shamelessness, fearlessness of wrongdoing, and restlessness accompany every unwholesome citta.

lessonSections.title: Unwholesome factors and the delusion group
body: The unwholesome mental factors comprise 14 cetasikas, divided into several groups.
Akusala (unwholesome) has five meanings: (1) diseased, bringing suffering; (2) unlovely, foul; (3) unskilful, clouded by greed-hatred-delusion; (4) faulty; (5) productive of painful results.

The delusion group (mocatuka) comprises four cetasikas: delusion (moha), shamelessness (ahirika), fearlessness of wrongdoing (anottappa) and restlessness (uddhacca). They are called 'unwholesome universals' because they accompany every unwholesome citta.
This section presents the Abhidhamma teaching on the relevant mental factors: their definitions, classifications and relationships as preserved in the source material.

sourceRefs.note: I/ TÂM SỞ SI PHẦN – MOCATUCACETASIKA; 5 nghĩa của Akusala

lessonSections.title: Shamelessness and Fearlessness of wrongdoing
body: Shamelessness (ahirika) is the lack of shame in doing wrong; fearlessness of wrongdoing (anottappa) is the lack of dread of wrongdoing. They always arise together.
This paragraph explains Anottappa: its characteristic, function, manifestation and proximate cause as taught in the Abhidhamma.

M3_TINH_HAO_BIEN_HANH.title: The twenty-five beautiful cetasikas
M3_TINH_HAO_BIEN_HANH.description: The nineteen beautiful universals present in every beautiful citta, plus the three abstinences, the two illimitables and the wisdom faculty.

lessonSections.title: The beautiful mental factors
body: Sobhana means 'shining, radiant, beautiful'. Beautiful factors are pure, good and skilful.
The beautiful mental factors number 25, divided into four groups: 19 beautiful universals, 3 abstinences, 2 illimitables and wisdom.
The 19 beautiful universals are present in every beautiful citta. They include faith, mindfulness, shame, dread, non-greed, non-hatred, equanimity and six pairs of mental and consciousness factors.

PC_01.name: Root condition
PC_01.definition: The six roots (hetu) support their associated mental states and the materiality produced by those roots, firmly the way roots sustain a tree.
PC_01.paccayaDhamma: The six roots: greed (lobha), hatred (dosa), delusion (moha), non-greed (alobha), non-hatred (adosa), non-delusion (amoha).
PC_01.paccayuppanna: The mind states associated with a root (citta and cetasikas), and the materiality that mind produces — mind-born materiality in the course of existence, kamma-born materiality at rebirth.
examples: A greed-rooted consciousness carries the two roots greed and delusion: together they make the whole mind-moment unwholesome.
A rootless (ahetuka) consciousness has no root and therefore receives no root condition — for example, the two receiving consciousnesses.
PC_01.doctrinalNote: Only the six root cetasikas are roots; however strong the other mental factors may be, they support their states only through other conditions.

PC_02.name: Object condition
PC_02.definition: An object supports mind and mental factors by serving as the thing known; without an object no consciousness arises.
PC_02.paccayaDhamma: The six objects: visible form, sound, odour, taste, tangible data, and mind objects (including Nibbāna and meditative attainments).
PC_02.paccayuppanna: All 89 cittas — every citta that knows an object — together with the 52 mental factors.
examples: A visible object (an image) serves as object condition for eye-consciousness and its associated mental factors.
Nibbāna serves as object condition for supramundane consciousness.
PC_02.doctrinalNote: According to Visuddhimagga XVII, ignorance serves as object condition for wholesome formations when a meditator examines ignorance with wisdom.

PC_03.name: Predominance condition
PC_03.definition: A dominant factor — the one given most weight in a moment — supports the states that arise with it; or an object, held predominant, supports the mind that takes it seriously.
PC_03.paccayaDhamma: The four conascent dominants — desire-to-act (chanda), energy (viriya), consciousness (citta), and investigation (vīmaṃsā, wisdom); and the predominant object.
PC_03.paccayuppanna: The mental states that arise together with a dominant; for the predominant object, the 84 cittas (excluding rootless resultant cittas) and their associated mental factors.

Sahajāt'ādhipati.name: Conascent dominance
Sahajāt'ādhipati.note: One of the four — desire, energy, consciousness, investigation — that stands out in a single mind-moment.

Ārammaṇ'ādhipati.name: Object dominance
Ārammaṇ'ādhipati.note: An object held predominant, governing the mind that takes it as its object.

examples: When a meditator's effort is at its strongest, energy predominates over the whole jhāna mind-moment.
A person besotted with a precious thing: that thing is the predominant object for the greedy mind.
PC_03.doctrinalNote: No predominance condition occurs among the 18 rootless cittas, nor in cittas where only one dominant is possible.

PC_04.name: Proximity condition
PC_04.definition: Mind and mental factors that have just ceased give way, and thereby support the arising of the immediately following mind and mental factors without interruption.
PC_04.paccayaDhamma: The consciousness and mental factors that have just ceased (except the dying consciousness of an Arahant).
PC_04.paccayuppanna: The mind and mental factors that arise immediately afterwards.
examples: Eye-consciousness, on ceasing, is proximity condition for the receiving consciousness in a five-door process.
The rebirth-linking consciousness, on ceasing, is proximity condition for the first life-continuum moment.
PC_04.doctrinalNote: Proximity condition underlies the continuity of the stream of consciousness — there is no gap between two mind-moments.

PC_05.name: Contiguity condition
PC_05.definition: Identical in meaning to proximity condition; it stresses immediate succession from mind-moment to mind-moment with nothing intervening.
PC_05.paccayaDhamma: The consciousness and mental factors that have just ceased.
PC_05.paccayuppanna: The mind and mental factors that follow immediately.
examples: The same relation is called proximity when spoken of as 'giving way', and contiguity when spoken of as 'following immediately'.
PC_05.doctrinalNote: These two conditions are one reality, differing only in presentation — like the two sides of a coin.

PC_06.name: Conascence condition
PC_06.definition: A state supports another state by arising together with it in one mind-moment, as three sticks propped against one another stand.
PC_06.paccayaDhamma: The four mental aggregates that arise together; the four great essentials; mind and its factors in the course of existence; and name and materiality at rebirth.
PC_06.paccayuppanna: The mental states conascent with one another, mind-born and kamma-born materiality in the course of existence, and the name–materiality that support one another at rebirth.
examples: In one greedy mind-moment, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness arise together and support one another.
At rebirth-linking, the rebirth consciousness and kamma-born materiality support each other through conascence condition.
PC_06.doctrinalNote: This is the condition most used to explain the simultaneity of name and materiality within a single mind-moment.

PC_07.name: Mutuality condition
PC_07.definition: Conascent states support one another reciprocally: each is at once the conditioning state and the conditioned state of the others.
PC_07.paccayaDhamma: The four conascent mental aggregates; the four great essentials; name and materiality at rebirth.
PC_07.paccayuppanna: Those very states — the relation is two-way.
examples: The four great essentials: the earth element supports the water element and the water element supports the earth — no element stands alone.
PC_07.doctrinalNote: Mutuality always accompanies conascence, but is narrower: materiality born of mind is not mutual with consciousness.

PC_08.name: Dependence condition
PC_08.definition: A state supports another by being its base or foothold, as a tree rests on the earth and a picture on its cloth.
PC_08.paccayaDhamma: The four conascent mental aggregates; the four great essentials; and the six bases (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and heart-base).
PC_08.paccayuppanna: The conascent mental states; derived materiality; and the seven consciousness-elements together with their mental factors.

Sahajāta-nissaya.name: Conascent dependence
Sahajāta-nissaya.note: Mutual reliance within a single mind-moment.

Purejāta-nissaya (vatthu).name: Prenascence dependence — bases
Purejāta-nissaya (vatthu).note: The six bases, arisen beforehand, serve as the support for the seven consciousness-elements.

Vatthārammaṇa-purejāta-nissaya.name: Base-object prenascence dependence
Vatthārammaṇa-purejāta-nissaya.note: The heart-base serves at once as base and as object for mind-element consciousness.

examples: The eye-base is dependence condition for eye-consciousness and its associated mental factors.
The heart-base (hadaya-vatthu) supports the whole mind-consciousness element throughout the life of the five aggregates.
PC_08.doctrinalNote: Distinguish from decisive support: dependence is the direct base, decisive support is strong assistance from a distance.

PC_09.name: Decisive support condition
PC_09.definition: A state supports another powerfully and decisively, as a particularly firm foothold that draws the mind after it.
PC_09.paccayaDhamma: An object strongly attended to; consciousness that has just ceased; and natural conditions such as faith, virtue, climate, food, and friends.
PC_09.paccayuppanna: The mind and mental factors that arise afterwards.

Ārammaṇ'ūpanissaya.name: Object decisive support
Ārammaṇ'ūpanissaya.note: A powerful object becomes the decisive spur for the consciousness that follows.

Anantar'ūpanissaya.name: Contiguous decisive support
Anantar'ūpanissaya.note: Equivalent to proximity condition considered as a force of support.

Pakat'ūpanissaya.name: Natural decisive support
Pakat'ūpanissaya.note: Natural conditions: faith, virtue, climate, friends, former kamma.

examples: Pleasant feeling is natural decisive support for craving — because feeling is agreeable, craving grows strong.
Faith decisively supports an act of generosity; greed decisively supports an act of stealing.
PC_09.doctrinalNote: The link Feeling → Craving in dependent origination is explained chiefly through natural decisive support.

PC_10.name: Prenascence condition
PC_10.definition: Materiality that has arisen earlier and still exists supports mental states that arise later, as the sun must exist before it can shine.
PC_10.paccayaDhamma: The six bases (materiality) and the six objects — the concrete material phenomena — that have already arisen.
PC_10.paccayuppanna: The mind and mental factors that arise later.

Vatthu-purejāta.name: Base prenascence
Vatthu-purejāta.note: The six bases support the seven consciousness-elements.

Ārammaṇa-purejāta.name: Object prenascence
Ārammaṇa-purejāta.note: Present concrete objects support the 54 sense-sphere cittas and 50 mental factors.

examples: The eye-base must exist first; only then can eye-consciousness arise.
A present visible object (17 mind-moments long) serves as prenascence condition for an eye-door process.
PC_10.doctrinalNote: Prenascence applies only to materiality; mental states cannot be prenascence conditions.

PC_11.name: Postnascence condition
PC_11.definition: Mental states that arise later support and sustain materiality that arose earlier, as rain nourishes a tree already planted.
PC_11.paccayaDhamma: The 85 cittas of the sense-sphere, form-sphere, formless-sphere and supramundane planes — that is, all consciousness except the rebirth-linking cittas — together with the 52 mental factors.
PC_11.paccayuppanna: The kamma-born body of materiality that arose earlier (the materiality of the living body).
examples: Mind and mental factors during life support the body already born, keeping it from decay.
Hunger drives one to eat — later-arising mentality nourishes earlier-born materiality.
PC_11.doctrinalNote: Only later-arising mentality supports earlier materiality; never the reverse.

PC_12.name: Repetition condition
PC_12.definition: An impulsion (javana) supports the impulsion that follows through repetition, so that the mind gathers strength moment after moment.
PC_12.paccayaDhamma: The preceding impulsion consciousness and its mental factors (except the final impulsion and the path impulsion).
PC_12.paccayuppanna: The impulsion consciousness and its factors arising immediately after.
examples: Among the seven impulsions, the first is repetition condition for the second.
Memorising by repeated recitation makes each later attempt easier — the same principle at work.
PC_12.doctrinalNote: A supramundane path impulsion is not repetition condition, because it arises for a single mind-moment only.

PC_13.name: Kamma condition
PC_13.definition: Volition (cetanā) supports its associated states and the materiality it produces, or supports results arising in other mind-moments.
PC_13.paccayaDhamma: Wholesome and unwholesome volition — the cetanā mental factor.
PC_13.paccayuppanna: Conascent kamma: the citta and cetasikas arising with it, and mind-born materiality. Asynchronous kamma: resultant consciousness, its mental factors, and kamma-born materiality at rebirth.

Sahajāta-kamma.name: Conascent kamma
Sahajāta-kamma.note: Volition supports the states arising with it in the same mind-moment.

Nānākkhaṇika-kamma.name: Asynchronous kamma
Nānākkhaṇika-kamma.note: Volition in one mind-moment supports its result in another — the basis of rebirth.

examples: Volition in an act of generosity supports resultant mind and kamma-born materiality in a future life (asynchronous kamma).
Volition in a greedy mind-moment makes that whole mind-moment unwholesome (conascent kamma).
PC_13.doctrinalNote: The links Formations → Consciousness and Becoming → Birth among the twelve links are explained through asynchronous kamma condition.

PC_14.name: Result condition
PC_14.definition: Resultant mental states support one another, and support kamma-born materiality, through their calm passivity — without any exertion.
PC_14.paccayaDhamma: The 36 resultant cittas (rootless, sense-sphere beautiful, and great resultants) together with their 38 associated mental factors.
PC_14.paccayuppanna: The resultant mental states that arise together, and the kamma-born materiality they produce.
examples: Rebirth-linking consciousness is a resultant: it supports the kamma-born materiality arising together with it.
Eye-consciousness is resultant mind — it supports its conascent mental factors by result condition without creating new kamma.
PC_14.doctrinalNote: Resultant consciousness creates no new kamma — the key point for understanding that 'a result does not produce a result'.

PC_15.name: Nutriment condition
PC_15.definition: A state nourishes other states so that they grow strong and endure.
PC_15.paccayaDhamma: Edible food (materiality) and the three mental nutriments: contact, volition, and consciousness.
PC_15.paccayuppanna: Food materiality sustains the body; the three mental nutriments sustain mind, mental factors, and mind-born materiality.

Nām'āhāra.name: Mental nutriment
Nām'āhāra.note: Contact, volition, and consciousness as nutriments.

examples: Food sustains the material body — edible food.
Volition nutriment: intention feeds kamma and prolongs the round of birth and death.
PC_15.doctrinalNote: Connect with the Four Nutriments in the Sutta Piṭaka (SN 12.63) — the contemplation of nutriment.

PC_16.name: Faculty condition
PC_16.definition: A faculty rules over its own domain, supporting its associated states or the states it governs.
PC_16.paccayaDhamma: The 20 faculties: five sensitive material faculties, the material life faculty, and fourteen mental faculties — feeling, faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, wisdom, the three understanding faculties, and the mind faculty.
PC_16.paccayuppanna: The sensitive faculties support the seven consciousness-elements; the mental faculties support the conascent mind and its factors; the material life faculty sustains kamma-born materiality.

Purejāta-indriya.name: Prenascence faculties
Purejāta-indriya.note: The five sensitive faculties support the consciousnesses they correspond to.

Jīvit'indriya.name: Material life faculty
Jīvit'indriya.note: Sustains the kamma-born materiality of its own group.

Sahajāta-indriya.name: Conascent faculties
Sahajāta-indriya.note: The fourteen mental faculties support the mind and factors arising with them.

examples: The eye faculty governs eye-consciousness — without the eye faculty there is no seeing.
The concentration faculty rules the whole jhāna mind-moment.
PC_16.doctrinalNote: The five spiritual faculties — faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, wisdom — must be balanced in meditation.

PC_17.name: Jhāna condition
PC_17.definition: The jhāna factors support their associated states by closely contemplating the object.
PC_17.paccayaDhamma: The seven jhāna factors: applied thought, sustained thought, rapture, pleasure, displeasure, equanimity, and one-pointedness.
PC_17.paccayuppanna: The associated mind and mental factors (except the two body consciousnesses), and the materiality produced by that mind.
examples: Applied thought brings the mind to the object — it is jhāna condition for the factors arising with it.
In the second jhāna applied thought is absent, yet rapture and one-pointedness still function as jhāna condition.
PC_17.doctrinalNote: Not limited to meditative attainment: the seven jhāna factors operate in ordinary consciousness as well.

PC_18.name: Path condition
PC_18.definition: The twelve path factors lead their associated states onward, as a road leads to its destination.
PC_18.paccayaDhamma: The twelve path factors: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration — and wrong view, wrong intention, wrong effort, wrong one-pointedness.
PC_18.paccayuppanna: The associated mind and mental factors (except the two body consciousnesses), and the materiality produced by that mind.
examples: Right view in a wholesome mind steers the whole mind-moment toward the wholesome.
Wrong view in a greedy mind steers it toward the unwholesome — path condition has two faces.
PC_18.doctrinalNote: Path condition operates in wholesome and unwholesome states alike — not only in the supramundane Noble Eightfold Path.

PC_19.name: Association condition
PC_19.definition: Mental states support one another through their union: one object, one base, arising and ceasing together.
PC_19.paccayuppanna: Those very four aggregates — a two-way relation.
examples: Feeling and perception in one mind-moment are associated: they know one object through one base.
PC_19.doctrinalNote: Only mentality can be associated; materiality has no shared object and base, so it cannot be associated.

PC_20.name: Dissociation condition
PC_20.definition: Mentality supports materiality, or materiality supports mentality, while remaining of a different kind — as water supports the lotus growing in it.
PC_20.paccayaDhamma: Mental states (when supporting materiality), or material phenomena (when supporting mentality).
PC_20.paccayuppanna: Material phenomena (conascent or prenascent), or mental states (conascent or postnascent).

Sahajāta-vippayutta.name: Conascent dissociation
Sahajāta-vippayutta.note: Mind and materiality arise together yet support each other as different kinds — at rebirth-linking.

Purejāta-vippayutta.name: Prenascence dissociation
Purejāta-vippayutta.note: The six bases, arisen earlier, support the seven consciousness-elements.

Pacchājāta-vippayutta.name: Postnascence dissociation
Pacchājāta-vippayutta.note: Later-arising mentality supports the earlier-born body of materiality.

examples: The heart-base (materiality) supports mind-consciousness (mentality) — different kinds, hence dissociation condition.
At rebirth-linking, the rebirth consciousness and kamma-born materiality arise together yet remain different kinds.
PC_20.doctrinalNote: This condition expresses the mind–matter relation, the backbone of the Name-and-Form analysis among the twelve links.

PC_21.name: Presence condition
PC_21.definition: A state that is present — whether conascent or prenascent — supports other states simply by being there.
PC_21.paccayaDhamma: Comprises the states serving as conascence, prenascence, postnascence, nutriment, and faculty conditions.
PC_21.paccayuppanna: The states supported by those five conditions.

Indriya-atthi.name: Faculty presence
Indriya-atthi.note: The material life faculty being present.

examples: The eye-base being present, eye-consciousness can arise — presence condition.
The four great essentials being present support the derived materiality.
PC_21.doctrinalNote: The widest of the 24 conditions — it subsumes five others.

PC_22.name: Absence condition
PC_22.definition: Mind and mental factors that have just ceased — precisely because they are no longer there — give room for the next consciousness to arise.
PC_22.paccayaDhamma: The consciousness and mental factors that have just ceased.
PC_22.paccayuppanna: The mind and mental factors arising immediately after.
examples: Eye-consciousness must cease for the receiving consciousness to arise.
PC_22.doctrinalNote: Same scope as proximity condition, but stressing the absence of the preceding consciousness.

PC_23.name: Disappearance condition
PC_23.definition: Identical in meaning to absence condition: a state, having gone, thereby supports the state that follows.
PC_23.paccayaDhamma: The consciousness and mental factors that have just ceased.
PC_23.paccayuppanna: The mind and mental factors arising immediately after.
examples: A life-continuum moment, just ceased (disappeared), supports the next life-continuum moment.
PC_23.doctrinalNote: One reality, two sayings: absence stresses 'no longer there'; disappearance stresses 'has gone'.

PC_24.name: Non-disappearance condition
PC_24.definition: Identical in meaning to presence condition: a state, not yet gone, keeps supporting the other states.
PC_24.paccayaDhamma: Comprises the states serving as conascence, prenascence, postnascence, nutriment, and faculty conditions.
PC_24.paccayuppanna: The states supported by those five conditions.
examples: The heart-base, not yet perished, keeps supporting mind-consciousness.
PC_24.doctrinalNote: The pairs 21–24 (presence / absence / disappearance / non-disappearance) close the 24 conditions with two pairs of synonyms.
